# **Metals Despatch** 

**Newsletter of the International Metals Study Groups** 

#### **December 2009, Issue No. 8** 

- It is anticipated that there will be a surplus in the world refined lead metal market of 80,000 tonnes in 2009 and just over 100,000 tonnes in 2010. 

##### **LEAD AND ZINC FORECAST** 

The outlook for World supply and demand for lead and zinc was presented during the ILZSG 54<sup>th</sup> Session held in Lisbon on 8 - 9 October 2009. Highlights include: 

   - Global **zinc usage** was forecast to decline 5.6% in 2009 to 10.76 million tonnes, the largest reduction since 1975, with only China and India increasing usage. The forecast for 2010 is 12.04 million tonnes, an increase of 11.92% over 2009. 

- **The global usage of refined lead** metal is expected to increase by 3.0% to 8.91 million tonnes for 2009 and by a further 7.5% in 2010. It is anticipated that 2009 demand in Europe will decline by 15.6% to its lowest level in 50 years and then partially recover by 8.8% in 2010. In the United States a contraction of 4.9% is forecast for 2009, followed by an increase of 2.9% in 2010. In China, increasing vehicle sales and production will see forecast growth in apparent demand of 25% in 2009 and a further 7.8% in 2010. 

   - Global **zinc mine output** is forecast to decrease to 11.08 million tonnes in 2009. Significant reductions are anticipated in Australia, China, Peru, Portugal and the United States. For 2010 mine output is predicted to grow by 8.1% to 11.97 million tonnes. 

   - **Global refined zinc production** is forecast to decline 4.7% to 11.14 million tonnes in 2009, then increase by 10.1% to 12.26 million tonnes in 2010. 

- Global **lead mine production** is forecast to increase by 1.3% to 3.94 million tonnes in 2009 with increased production in China being offset by reductions in output in Australia, Canada and Peru. For 2010 the forecast is for an increase of 5.8% to 4.17 million tonnes. 

   - The latest **forecasts** supplied by the Group’s member countries indicate that global supply of refined zinc metal will exceed demand by 380,000 tonnes in 2009 and 227,000 tonnes in 2010. 

- Globally, production of **refined lead metal** output in 2009 is expected to increase by 3.4% to 8.99 million tonnes. In 2010, a predicted increase of 7.4% will be driven primarily by the commissioning of new plants in Brazil and India and higher production in China, Germany, Italy, Japan and the United States. 

For further details of the outcomes of the ILZSG meetings or questions on the market outlook please email Paul White at <u>paul_white@ilzsg.org</u>

##### **NICKEL FORECAST** 

The International Nickel Study Group (INSG) met on 5 - 6 October 2009 in Lisbon and reviewed the current outlook for trends in World supply and demand for nickel in the context of the economic crisis and issued the following forecast: 

- Global **primary nickel usage** (consumption) was 1.29 Mt in 2008 and forecast to decline to 1.21 Mt in 2009. For 2010 a recovery to 1.35Mt is envisaged. 

- World **primary refined nickel production** was 1.38 Mt in 2008, and set to decline to 1.28 Mt in 2009. In 2010 production is anticipated to increase to 1.44 Mt. The 2009 and 2010 figures do not include any general adjustment factor for possible production disruptions. 

- INSG also discussed **market trends** and noted that a recovery in stainless steel production started in China, Korea and Taiwan, China in the second quarter of this year and to lesser extent in Europe and the United States in the third quarter. Primary nickel demand was strong in China and surrounding countries, with both real and apparent consumption increasing. In Europe and the United States demand is expected to decline in 2009 due to weak stainless steel production and also relatively high usage of nickel-containing scrap. In 2010 it is possible that growth in stainless steel and nickel use will

continue in China and in other parts of the world but at slower rate. 

INSG recognizes that the current global economic crisis has created a large degree of uncertainty in the global market, and its impacts on both the supply and demand for nickel are not fully known.  The Study Group cautions that future market developments 

could significantly alter the forward-looking market balance. 

For further details of the outcomes of the INSG meetings or questions on the market outlook please email Sven Tollin at sven.tollin@insg.org 

##### **JOINT STUDY GROUPS’ SEMINAR** 

The International Lead and Zinc Study Group (ILZSG), the International Copper Study Group (ICSG) and the International Nickel Study Group (INSG), held a Joint Seminar on “Post-Crisis Metals: What will be Different?” on 7 October 2009 in Lisbon. 

Mr. Paulo de Sa, Manager, Oil and Gas Division of the World Bank gave the opening presentation on the Outlook for the Global Economy and Implications for Mining and Metals. Mr.Shang Fushan of China Nonferrous Metal Industry Association spoke on the outlook for China.  Presentations on the situation facing the copper, lead and zinc and nickel industries, followed by a panel discussion, were made by Mr. Neil Buxton of GFMS Consulting, Mr. Robin Bhar of Calyon and Mr. Jim Lennon of Macquarie. Mr. Magnus Ericcson of Raw Materials Group spoke on post crisis industry structures and M&A activity. Mr. Duan Shaopau of CNIA spoke on the challenges and opportunities facing China’s metal industries. Representatives from Australia and the European Commission provided important contributions. Among the conclusions of the seminar was agreement that greater transparency in metals markets is needed to assist in responding to economic crises. The seminar was followed by a reception hosted by the RBS Sempra Commodities. For further details about work underway in the Study Groups please email paul_white@ilzsg.org (for lead and zinc), <u>curtis_stewart@ilzsg.org</u> (for nickel) and <u>risopatron@icsg.org</u> (for copper).  The presentations given at the Seminar may be viewed by visiting: <u>http://www.ilzsg.org/presentations.asp</u> 

##### **INSG MEETING 5-6 OCTOBER 2009** 

Delegates from INSG member countries, industry and observing countries/organisations met in Lisbon 5 - 6 October to review statistical, economic and environmental issues related to nickel. 

Delegates reviewed the INSG primary nickel market statistics in detail, and discussed the market forecast, which was prepared by the secretariat based on information provided by governments and industry. Details of the forecasts are provided above. 

The INSG Environmental and Economic Committee received presentations on topics related to environmental regulation and international policy initiatives that may affect nickel. Mr Stephen Barnett, President of the Nickel Institute gave a presentation on ‘REACH, Regulatory and Other Issues Affecting Nickel’ and Mr. Sylvain Bintein from DG Environment,

The Statistics Committee, in addition to reviewing the latest statistical data, also received valuable input to its work through a series of presentations and discussions. 

Mr. Markus Moll, Managing Director & Senior Market Analyst of SMR: Steel & Metals Research, Austria, made a presentation on “Market Drivers for Nickelalloys”. Mr. Bian Gang, China Non-Ferrous Metals Industry Association (CNIA), China, made a presentation on “Nickel in China”. A presentation provided by Mr. Peter Kaumanns, ISSF, Belgium, on latest developments in the world stainless steel market was delivered on his behalf. 

The INSG Industry Advisory Panel, comprised of representatives from the world’s nickel producing, consuming and recycling industries, provided valuable input on the Study Group’s work program priorities. The Panel heard presentations from: Mr Denis Lencou-Bareme of Eramet who discussed global nickel supply and demand, Mr. Benno Kratz from ELG, Germany, who gave a presentation on stainless steel scrap, and Mr. Michael Widmer of Bank of America-Merrill Lynch who spoke on nickel pig iron in China. 

Copies of the presentations are available on the INSG website www.insg.org 

##### **ICSG CONVENES 34**<sup>**th**</sup> **REGULAR MEETING** 

Over 50 representatives from ICSG member governments and companies, observer governments and organizations attended the International Copper Study Group’s 34<sup>th</sup> Regular Meeting at ICSG Headquarters in Lisbon on 5-6 October 2009. 

Meetings were held of the Statistical Committee, Environmental and Economic Committee and Standing Committee. At the Statistical Committee meeting, ICSG Chief Statistician Ana Rebelo delivered a presentation on the accuracy of ICSG forecasts as well as the ICSG copper production and usage forecast for 2009/2010, which was followed by the Forecasting Forum. Other highlights of the Statistical Committee meeting included a presentation by Ms Susanna Keung, Consultant at CRU, on recent trends in copper wirerod markets and a presentation by ICSG Economist Joe Pickard on the 2009 ICSG World Copper Factbook. 

At the Environmental and Economic Committee (EEC) meeting the Committee was provided with two different presentations at the Workshop on Policy and Incentives for Copper Scrap Trade, Recycling and Use by Mr Stefan-Georg Fuchs, Head of Electronic Scrap Procurement, Aurubis AG and by Mr Michael Widmer, Metals Strategist, Bank of 

America/Merrill Lynch. In addition, ICSG Head of Environment and Economics Mr Carlos Risopatron presented an update of the ICSG Copper Scrap Project and the final report of the project on Constraints on Copper Supply Coming On Stream. Members approved a project on Leading Economic Indicators of Refined Copper Usage and were informed of other recent work

including the update of the China copper and alloys semis production database, the 2009 report on regulations affecting copper use, reuse and trade, and Common Fund for Commodities’ projects. Presentations may be viewed at ICSG’s web site www.icsg.org 

##### **ICSG CHINA COPPER MARKET SEMINAR AND CNIA/ANTAIKE CHINA INTERNATIONAL COPPER CONFERENCE 2009** 

Nearly 350 participants attended these groundbreaking meetings held on 6-8 November 2009 in Wuhan, China. Presentations were delivered by ICSG Chairman Mr Erik Heimlich (Chile), Chairman of the ICSG Environmental and Economic Committee Ms Ajita Bajpai Pande (India), the ICSG Secretary-General and ICSG Heads of Statistics, Environment and Economics, representatives from CNIA and Antaike, Chinese government and industry representatives on a range of topics related to the Chinese and global copper markets. View the presentations at <u>www.icsg.org</u> 



##### **ICSG IAP MEETS DURING LONDON LME WEEK** 

The ICSG Industry Advisory Panel met on 15 October in London with the objective of encouraging further industry participation and informing a wider range of copper industry representatives of the work and benefits of the Study Group. Industry advisers from Australia, Chile, Germany, Italy, Japan, Poland, Portugal, Spain, Sweden and the United States were present along with industry association, government and Study Group representatives. The IAP provides an opportunity for industry advisers to meet as a group, raise issues for the attention of government members and provide feedback and guidance to the Group on its priorities, programs and activities.

##### **_INSG Nickel in Batteries 2009_** 

A comprehensive report on the use of nickel in batteries drawing on data from a variety of sources, both government and private.  Provides a history of nickel in batteries and describes the principal types of batteries which use nickel. A comparison of the various nickel containing batteries in terms of cost and energy density is provided, as is information on the environmental regulations impacting nickel batteries. Includes a list of major producers of nickel containing batteries with web addresses. 25 Pages. _Published May 2009_ . 

##### **_INSG Environment, Health and Safety (EHS) Regulations Relating to Nickel 2009_** 

A compilation of environmental, health and safety regulations affecting nickel. The listing is provided by country, state or province as well as international regulations.  It is presented in a spreadsheet format and contains web links to regulations in various jurisdictions. 42 pages. _Published June 2009_ .
